FACILITY DESCRIPTION The Permittee owns and operates a wastewater treatment, recycling, and disposal facility which provides sewerage services 384 connections, serving a population of approximately 930, including residential, commercial, and institutional customers in the Forestville and Mirabel Heights Zone of Benefit (Mirabel Heights) area. There are no industrial users that discharge into the Facility. The Permittee’s wastewater makeup is approximately 65 percent residential flow, 21 percent commercial flow, and 14 percent institutional flow. The institutional portion reflects two schools, which serve larger populations than live within the Permittee’s service area. The Facility is designed to provide advanced wastewater treatment for an average dry weather flow of 0.130 mgd, and a peak weekly wet weather flow of 0.576 mgd. 2.1.1. chunks.citation: Shin, C et al. (2021). Anaerobic membrane bioreactor model for design and prediction of domestic wastewater treatment process performance. CHEM ENG J.
chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: In order to recover the lipid-rich biomass from the treated wastewaters and to further reduce the level of COD in the respective wastewaters, microfiltration using a low-cost ceramic membrane (pore size: 1.01 μm and porosity: 44%) was carried out. Fig. 6 presents the membrane flux and COD removal (%) from the different wastewaters at various operating pressures in the range of 34-172 kPa. With an increase in the operating pressure, the flux of the microfiltration system increased due to a high driving force acting on the membrane surface. The membrane flux was lower for DWW and PPWW as compared with that for the BGWW due to membrane fouling. In general, the membrane fouling is attributed to concentration polarization on the membrane surface and blocking of pores in the porous ceramic structure. In case of DWW and PPWW, fouling of the membrane was observed due to the adsorption of organic solutes/lignin and membrane surface polarization that creates further resistance to the transport of liquid through the membrane [1] . On the other hand, the less viscous BGWW possesses persistent organics [22] , and hence do not affect the membrane flux largely.

A study conducted by the Water Environment and Reuse Foundation sought to determine whether ORP or FC is better suited to control chlorine dosing in wastewater treatment plant effluents (WERF, 2005) . The study concludes that for the chlorination of wastewater treatment plant effluents no technology was clearly superior for all criteria considered (provide information to meet effluent requirements; provide process control system reliability; minimize requirements; and minimize chemical use). However, ORP had a lower correlation with fecal coliforms in the chlorinated water. The main reason stated for the poorer performance of ORP were fluctuations of the ORP in the wastewater (between ~200 mV and 500 mV), as a result of the weather conditions (dry vs. wet) and of industrial discharge. We expect the influent composition of decentralized water reuse systems to be less variable (no dependency on the weather, no industrial input), however, this needs confirmation from field campaigns.

chunks.text: Although concentrations of lesser chlorinated ethenes were not measured during this trial, the absence of prolonged DCE accumulation in the bioreactor system indicated that dechlorination progressed beyond the DCE level. Overall, stable TCE removal rates >90% were demonstrated by both R1 and R3 at all influent TCE concentrations, with effluent TCE concentrations frequently below the detectable limit (10 lg l À1 ; Table 1 ). These results are comparable with previous studies of the treatment of chlorinated alkenes, which reported efficient removal of tetrachloroethene (PCE) up to concentrations of 50 mg l À1 in an upflow anaerobic sludge bed bioreactor, operated at room temperature (Prakash and Gupta, 2000) , and 98% PCE removal using an anaerobic attached film expanded bed (AA-FEB) process operating at low temperature, but only up to a loading rate of 12 mg l À1 (Carter and Jewell, 2003) .

chunks.citation: Silva-Gálvez, AL et al. (2024). Strategies for livestock wastewater treatment and optimised nutrient recovery using microalgal-based technologies. J ENVIRON MANAGE.
chunks.text: Anaerobic digestion (AD), an anoxic biological wastewater treatment process, is widely implemented to reduce the organic load of LW. It was the third most used process in the selected references. During AD, a gas mixture (biogas) and an effluent (digestate) are produced. The biogas, primarily composed of CH 4 and CO 2 , can be used to produce energy. The effluent, known as digestate or anaerobically digested livestock wastewater (ADLW), requires further treatment before being reused or discharged due to its high content of organic matter, N, P, and pathogens (Huo et al., 2021) . Wang et al. (2022a) conducted a full-scale microalgal electroactive wetland coupled with AD to treat SW. The AD achieved removal efficiencies of 77-89% CODr, 27-30% TPr, 26-73% NH 4 + -N removal, and 50-63% TNr. These efficiencies were temperature-dependent, with higher values in summer and spring, and lower in autumn and winter.

chunks.citation: Mu, DY et al. (2016). A life cycle assessment and economic analysis of the Scum-to-Biodiesel technology in wastewater treatment plants. BIORESOURCE TECHNOL.
chunks.text: Presently, there are approximately 21,600 municipal wastewater treatment facilities serving 226.4 million people (USEPA, 2008) in the U.S. A large amount of biosolids including sludge and scum from these facilities are generated and then disposed either in landfills (28%) or in farmlands (45%, Willis et al., 2012) . This biosolid management practice has caused many environmental pollution and economic stress because biosolids landfilling raises disposal fee for the wastewater treatment facilities and releases methane as a strong greenhouse gas in landfills. Current research shows those biosolid wastes contain a good deal of energy. For example, the sludge collected from the primary and secondary treatment processes contains the energy of 8000 Btu per dry pound and scum contains 11,400 Btu per dry pound (Outwater, 1994; McCarty et al., 2011) . By recovering, utilizing, or selling the energy contained in those wastes, wastewater treatment facilities can reduce not only a large amount of waste disposal to landfills, eliminate the operation cost associated with the old practice, but generate extra revenue for better economic and societal benefit.

chunks.text: We focus on two scales: a catchment scale and a cluster scale. 24 A catchment is defined as the service area of a centralized wastewater treatment plant (CTP). Resource recovery at this scale requires a wastewater collection system, a CTP, a system for storage and distribution of treated water, and a system for energy recovery from organic matter. We subdivide the catchment into "clusters", collections of buildings that share a sewer line (e.g., a homeowner's association, a small city, campus). Resource recovery at this scale requires removal of wastewater from the catchment collection system (a practice referred to as "scalping" and requiring a scalping system including a pump station); treatment at a satellite treatment plant (STP); return of residuals to the collection system; a system for storage and distribution of treated water; and the possibility of a system for energy recovery from organic matter. For this study, we restrict delivery of reclaimed water to the clusters from which the wastewater originated. For our case study, the catchment is that of the PARWQCP.

chunks.text: Based on a survey on pre-treatment measures for 17 full-scale AeMBRs, the following information deserves special attention (Itokawa et al., 2008) : 1) grit chamber, coarse and fine screenings are mostly essential for MBR operation to removal grits, large suspended particles and long fibers, with fine screening (3 mm for FS membrane and 0.5-1 mm for HF membrane) installed universally; and 2) using the "by pass sieving" method, which recycles part of the suspended sludge through a sieve, achieves the further removal of unfavorable substances accumulated in the bioreactor. These means can be extended to AnMBRs minimizing the presence of undesirable substances into the bioreactor while with adequate consideration of keeping strict anaerobic environment. A recent novel concept, referred to as wastewater pre-concentration (Ansari et al., 2016) , is still under investigation, but has shown great potential to enhance bioresource recovery and energy generation efficiency (Guven et al., 2019) , accompanied by a low volumetric flow rate and process footprint (Alvarado et al., 2020) .

chunks.text: Nitrogen removal in conventional wastewater treatment is primarily accomplished through nitrification/denitrification (N/DN) (Arumugham et al., 2024) . However, this process requires aeration and carbon sources, and produces CO 2 and N 2 O (Cao and Fan, 2023) . Wastewater treatment facilities produce 1-2 % of society's total carbon dioxide emissions (Zhang et al., 2024b) , and 3 % of global N 2 O (Ramírez-Melgarejo et al., 2020) . In contrast, anammox utilizes nitrite as an electron acceptor to directly convert NH 4 + to N 2 , reducing N 2 O emissions, reducing oxygen consumption by 62.5 %, eliminating the need for carbon inputs, and reducing sludge production by 90 % (Huang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2019a) .

chunks.text: A pilot scale ceramic cross flow microfiltration (MF) system (Fig. 1 ) was used for pig manure filtration. The MF system primarily consisted of controlling valves, pumps, membrane modules, manometer, flowmeters, thermometer, temperature controller and a programmable logical controller (PLC) system. An external tank of 100 L volume was used as feed tank for the experiment. A ceramic MF membrane (Al 2 O 3 , inopore GmbH, Germany) module of 0.2 µm pore size and 1 m Length was used for the filtration. The effective membrane area was 0.158 m 2 .

chunks.citation: Guo, KH et al. (2018). Comparison of the UV/chlorine and UV/H2O2 processes in the degradation of PPCPs in simulated drinking water and wastewater: Kinetics, radical mechanism and energy requirements. WATER RES.
chunks.text: In pure water, among the investigated 28 PPCPs, the UV/H 2 O 2 process was superior to the UV/chlorine process for the removal of 12 PPCPs primarily driven by HO at neutral pH values, while the UV/chlorine process was better for the other 16 PPCPs primarily driven by the RCS. The concentration of HO was lower in the UV/ chlorine process than in the UV/H 2 O 2 process, but RCS such as Cl and ClO in UV/chlorine contributed to the degradation of PPCPs with electron-donating functional groups. ClO was important to the degradation of PPCPs possessing electron-rich groups in the UV/chlorine process. The steady-state concentration of ClO was calculated to be ~3 orders of magnitude greater than that of HO , and the reactivities of ClO with 16 PPCPs were determined to be in the range of 10 6 e10 9 M À1 s À1 . The reactivity of ClO (ln k ClO ) was linearly related to the Hammett Ss pþ constant for aromatic PPCPs.
